title: Your Son Is Not the Problem. His Youth Group Might Be.
author: Anthony B. Bradley
summary: Anthony B. Bradley argues that adolescent boys who resist church youth ministry are typically responding rationally to a ministry culture structured for girls rather than for them—one featuring silly games, sharing circles, and leaders who lack the masculine gravitas that young men admire. Drawing on the four masculine archetypes of King, Warrior, Sage, and Lover, he contends that boys are drawn to men who are impressive, serious, intense, and articulate—men they aspire to become—not to 'cool' charismatic leaders running Cheeto Face games. His prescriptive solution is for fathers to bypass inadequate youth ministries and form their own cohorts: groups of fathers meeting with their sons for challenging shared activities, demanding Socratic discussions of scripture and culture, and real food, led by men the boys genuinely respect. He warns that forcing boys to attend ineffective youth group drives them toward nominalism, while boys from dad-deprived homes are the ones who most need access to a multi-generational brotherhood of serious men. The essay concludes that online influencers in the 'manosphere' are filling a vacuum left by churches that offer no compelling model of manhood.
points: Most youth ministries are structured for girls—with sharing circles, silly games, and charismatic-but-unimpressive male leaders—in ways that rationally repel boys who want intensity, depth, and aspirational formation.

Middle-school and high-school boys are drawn to men who embody the King, Warrior, Sage, and Lover archetypes: authoritative, courageous, discerning, and passionate men who will challenge them and call them to greatness.

Fathers who are not themselves awe-inspired by their son's youth pastor should not force the boy to attend—bribery and coercion make things worse and accelerate drift toward nominalism after high school.

A father-led cohort model—challenging shared activities, adult-level Socratic discussions of scripture and culture, real food—can provide the formative environment boys crave without any institutional permission required.

The manosphere is filling a vacuum left by churches that fail to offer a compelling model of manhood; blaming online influencers without asking why church leaders produced an inferior alternative misidentifies the problem.
quotes: Middle-school and high-school boys are drawn to impressive men. They are drawn to men who represent the kind of men they aspire to become. They want to be around aspirational men: men who are smart, serious, intense, rigorous, and articulate; men who will challenge them intellectually and call them to greatness in mind, body, and soul.

Most youth ministries are structured for girls, not boys. Too often, the male leaders lack the masculine gravitas, competence, and strength that adolescent boys admire. This is why the games are silly rather than demanding.

Fathers, here is the bottom line: if you are not awe-inspired by the men leading your son's youth ministry, and your son shows no interest in attending, do not force him to go. You are making it worse for everyone.

Your sons want to be around Kings, Warriors, Sages, and Lovers. The best resources for middle-school and high-school boys in the church are the other men in the church. Every church has men who have been tested in these areas and have thrived.

Boys from broken homes need a multi-generational brotherhood exponentially more than they need to play 'Cheeto Face.' Fathers, do not waste your sons' middle-school and high-school years by subjecting them to men who do not impress you.

Boys are turning to online influencers because many of those men project strength, competence, seriousness, and aspiration. Do not blame the 'manosphere' without asking why church leaders have failed to offer a more compelling model of manhood.
